accepted.name: price_is_unpriced
accepted.description: Flags the 0.0 price sentinel: a catalogue row with no list price recorded, not a free item. Separates 'price unknown' from 'price low', which a model fed raw price cannot distinguish.
accepted.why_it_matters: item-ltv is dollars = price x future purchases, so a product whose price field is the missing-value sentinel has a structurally different (near-zero or uninformative) label scale; the raw column silently puts it at the bottom of the price axis instead.

accepted.name: price_cents_ending
accepted.description: The cents part of the list price, 0-99. Not a rescaling of price: it is non-monotone in price and isolates the pricing convention (.99, .95, .00) from the price level.
accepted.why_it_matters: price endings encode who set the price - consumer retail charm points vs publisher/wholesale round numbers - and only 8,679 distinct prices cover 506k products, so the ending is a real categorical signal about listing provenance and expected demand.

accepted.name: charm_priced
accepted.description: Charm (psychological) pricing flag: the price ends in .90-.99, i.e. the .99/.95 points typical of consumer retail listings.
accepted.why_it_matters: charm-priced items are actively merchandised to consumers and so attract the steady trickle of purchases that drives 3-month LTV; the median (12.99) and p25 (8.99) prices sit here, but p75 (17.59) does not, so the flag is not a monotone cut of price.

accepted.name: round_dollar_priced
accepted.description: A real price that is a whole number of dollars. Whole-dollar listings in a book-like catalogue are typically wholesale, institutional or hand-entered rather than retail-merchandised; the (price > 0) term excludes the 0.0 missing sentinel, which is also integral.
accepted.why_it_matters: distinguishes a catalogue entry that was priced by a retail pricing rule from one that was not, a provenance difference that predicts whether the item sells continuously or sporadically - and it needs the sentinel exclusion, which no pairwise generator will add.

accepted.name: high_ticket_item
accepted.description: High-ticket flag: list price at or above $50, roughly mean + 0.8 sd of a distribution whose p75 is 17.59.
accepted.why_it_matters: price has std 43 against mean 16 with a max of 5,204, so for a dollar-valued target a handful of expensive items dominate the loss; marking the tail membership explicitly is different information from the tail value itself.

accepted.name: verified_rating
accepted.description: The star rating kept only when the review came from a verified purchase, 0 otherwise. A trust-gated rating level.
accepted.why_it_matters: only a verified review is evidence that money changed hands, which is exactly what LTV sums; an unverified 5-star is a marketing artifact. The brute-force generator tries rating - verified and rating / verified, never the product that implements the gate.

accepted.name: verified_sentiment
accepted.description: Signed sentiment of a verified purchase: positive for 4-5 stars, negative for 1-2, zero for neutral and zero for every unverified review.
accepted.why_it_matters: collapses 'no credible opinion' and 'credible but neutral' onto the same zero while letting credible dissatisfaction push negative - the valence counterpart to verified_rating, which cannot go below zero.

accepted.name: nps_contribution
accepted.description: Net-Promoter-style contribution of one review: +1 promoter (4-5 stars), 0 passive (3 stars), -1 detractor (1-2 stars).
accepted.why_it_matters: ratings are a 1-5 ordinal label, not a measurement, and their distribution is pathological (mean 4.39, median 5, half the mass on 5); the promoter/detractor coding is the standard way practitioners turn that skew into a usable per-review quantity, and arithmetic differences on the raw label do not.

accepted.name: verified_nps_contribution
accepted.description: Promoter/detractor contribution counted only for verified purchases; unverified reviews contribute 0 instead of a vote.
accepted.why_it_matters: 30% of reviews are unverified and those are where incentivized praise and retaliatory one-stars concentrate; this is the per-review term whose sum over a product's history is the credible word-of-mouth balance driving future purchases.

accepted.name: rating_extremity
accepted.description: How far from neutral the rating is, ignoring direction: 0 for 3 stars, 1 for 2/4, 2 for 1/5. Opinion strength rather than opinion sign.
accepted.why_it_matters: polarization and valence are different properties of a product's review stream - a contested item and a blandly-liked item can share a mean rating - and no difference or ratio of raw columns recovers the folded distance.

accepted.name: unverified_extreme_review
accepted.description: The fake/incentivized-review signature: a 1-star or 5-star rating with no verified purchase behind it.
accepted.why_it_matters: the conjunction is the heuristic practitioners actually use to discount a review stream; either condition alone is common and uninformative (69.5% verified, ~half of all ratings are 5), so the signal exists only in the product of the two, which requires knowing that verified is a provenance flag and rating is an ordinal label.
